column2: A mine cross-section. Both rows start as solid rock (ROM 0xFF blocks, with ore glints drawn in CGRAM), and the time is a tunnel: the digits are the hollow galleries a little miner with a head lamp has dug, so the numerals are negative space carved out of the glass. The miner swings a pick (chips fly as tiles), pushes a mine cart along the tunnel, and his lamp is the only bright spot. On the minute he backfills the old gallery with rubble from the cart and digs the new one stroke by stroke; on the hour dynamite: a fuse fizzes along the rock, a flash, dust settling (the slow glass is the dust), and the whole new hour is blown open at once.

A samurai duel. A swordsman stands in the wind (a falling-petal tile drifts across both rows), facing the time: big two-row numerals made of brush-stroke tiles. At :59 he draws, the glass freezes for a beat, a single blinding slash streaks across the row (the LC lag makes the after-image), and the old digit slides apart in two halves along the cut, cell by cell, falling away; the new digit is sheathed into place stroke by stroke as he returns the sword. Idle: hand on the hilt, breathing, petals, a flick of the eyes. Hour: two swordsmen, a flurry of clashing slashes.

A zipper. Row seams become zipper teeth: two rows of interlocking teeth tiles run across the glass, and the time lives in fabric that is revealed when the zipper opens. A slider with a pull-tab (hand-drawn, swinging with momentum) runs along the teeth: each minute it unzips the changing part, the teeth splay apart into a V, the old digit is folded away inside, the new one is printed on the lining underneath, and it zips shut again with a satisfying shimmy. Idle: the pull-tab dangles and sways, a loose thread flutters. Hour: the whole strip unzips end to end like a jacket and something peeks out.

A prison yard at night (or a jewel museum): the glass is dark and the time is painted on the wall but can only be seen where a sweeping searchlight passes. The beam is a few cells wide, sweeping back and forth, and the slow glass is the afterglow: digits glow in the beam and fade behind it like phosphor. A tiny thief in a striped shirt tiptoes across, freezes and flattens against the wall when the beam comes, shuffles the old digit away and paints the new one while the light is elsewhere. The time must be readable at least once per sweep (sweep fast enough). Hour: alarm, two beams cross, sirens blink.

Fishing off a pier. The top row is the sky and the pier with a little angler sitting on a bucket, rod over the water; the bottom row is under the water, where fish shaped like (and carrying) digits swim lazily, the time is the four fish holding position in their slots, fins fluttering. Bobber bobs, ripples. On the minute the bobber dips, the angler strikes, the old digit-fish is reeled up flapping, thrown into the bucket (splash), and a new fish swims into the slot from the side. Hour: a huge fish pulls the angler in.

A construction site. A tower crane's jib runs along the top row with a trolley and a hook on a cable; the time is a building on the bottom row whose floors and girders form big brick-and-steel numerals (custom tiles, rivets, hard-hat workers). Idle: the trolley creeps, the hook sways like a pendulum, a worker waves, a welder's spark flickers. Minute: the crane lifts the old digit's girders off one by one and lowers new ones into place, the hook swinging with real lag; a worker guides it in. Hour: a topping-out ceremony, a tiny tree hoisted to the top and a flag.

A street juggler. A little juggler stands in the middle and the time is the balls in the air: the four digits, drawn as round ball tiles, ride juggling arcs above their hands across both rows (cascade patterns, each digit pausing at the peak of its arc where you read it). The pattern is always going, hands toss and catch with real timing. On the minute the juggler tosses the old digit off-stage and a new ball is thrown in from the crowd, caught without dropping the pattern. Hour: a cascade of clubs, a pirouette, a bow and applause.

A rooftop pigeon loft. Pigeons (round chests, bobbing heads, hand-drawn with personality) sit on a wire across the top row; each digit of the time is a message envelope or a big numeral sign they are perched on, coo and peck. Idle: head bobbing, wing stretch, one pigeon edging along the wire. On the minute a carrier pigeon flaps in with a new number in its beak, there is a squabble, the old card falls flutter-down off the bottom row and the new one is hung up. Hour: the whole flock takes off and circles, landing again in the new order.
